en: O India, your tainted heap of dust—
as long as the sea does not swallow it, so long must you weep.
As long as these snow-peaks, touching the sky—the storied glory of the ancient Hindu—
stand at your bedside and flood your breast with tears,
so long must you weep.
The day that has gone from you will never come again.
The sun that has sunk in the west will rise in the east no more.
Such base, mean-spirited children of shame have been born to you
that not one of them sheds a single drop of tears for you.
When the day that poured out blood for you has gone away,
then, India, weep.
Then why, Fate, have you kept India's body decked in so many ornaments?
Birds sing in India's forests, India's sky is smeared with golden clouds—
here the vines are laden with flowers, here the earth is rich with golden grain—
the joyous river flows along.
Why, shameless, do you wear ornaments, filling a disease-wasted face with heaps of smiles,
and boast, alas, of your beauty?
The day that has gone will not return,
so then, O India, weep.
India, seeing this shame of yours, hiding our faces darkened with disgrace,
we poets would weep in solitude, in solitude strike our veenas in sorrow,
yet when even in that there is no freedom,
then, India, weep.
O sorrowful veena, come, my friend, sing those old songs of yore—
fill this darkened soul with dreams long hidden away.
Ah, cruel fate, do you remember—there was once such a day
when I, Lakshmi of the Aryans, on this Himalaya, this charming veena in my hand,
sang such a song that the world, hearing it, started in wonder.
I suckled Arjuna—I suckled Yudhishthira at my breast.
Sitting in this lap, Valmiki sang the holy Ramayana.
Today I am luckless—today an orphan
in fear, in fear, hiding, hiding, I weep in silence, in silence,
lest, hearing the mother's weeping, a single child should wake!
Fate does not allow me even to weep.
Alas, God, they do not know that day has passed away
when, to wipe a single teardrop, what would my children not have done—
how much blood they would have poured out.
Hear, oh hear our anguish, God of gods, Lord, merciful one—
our eyes are streaming, our hearts are breaking.
Darkness does not last forever—the sun rises, the night departs—
will this midnight over this land's head never wane?
Will our eyes stream forever? Will our hearts break forever?
So much sorrow hidden in the heart's core, we keep our pale faces covered—
no leisure even to weep—no words, only the breast breaking.
The soul shrinks and languishes, terror fills the ten directions—
in a land so low and destitute, perhaps you will make no home.
Our eyes will stream forever, our hearts will break forever.
Shall we ever lift our heads? Will the senseless soul awaken?
Will your song of triumph rise in India's morning sky?
Nowhere, on no day, do we hear a word of comfort—
so we all wait, longing to hear your voice.
Say, Lord, that these eyes will be wiped, that the heart will not break forever.
What darkness is this over the land of India!
It seems, Father, you have forsaken her.
Moment by moment she sinks into the abyss—who will deliver her?
I look on every side and see no way out. No shelter anywhere, utterly helpless.
Today, in this darkness, in this sea of peril, whose feet shall she clasp?
Look upon her, Father, end this sorrow. Do not turn away from this hapless land—
else, in darkness, in the sea of peril, whose feet shall she clasp?
Look down: your thousand children, heads bowed in shame, trembling with fear,
weeping, enduring a hundred insults—no shame, no honor remains.
They have lifted debasement onto their heads, and so have forgotten even you;
they no longer call on you with yearning hearts as the merciful one.
Look, Father, look, oh look. End this sin of debasement, this sorrow.
Wipe away, wipe away the stain from her brow—else this land cannot survive.
When you dwelt in this holy house, what nectar of fragrance rode the wind,
what songs of joy rose into the sky, what light of genius blazed!
In India's forests the sages' songs journeyed toward the eternal abode—
gazing toward you, all walked together along the holy path.
What has become of her today! Look, Father, look. End this anguish, this sin, this sorrow.
We remain your children still,
though we have fallen.
Veil your face, O moon, in the clouds.
Birds, be still, be still. Weep in the darkness, O earth.
If you must sing, then sing, all of you—sing with the mighty roar of a hundred thunderbolts—
with a terrible song of doomsday waken, waken, oh waken this India.
Forest bird, sing no more that song of pleasure. Pouring the wine of delight from soul to soul,
why does the melody of joy play so gladly today—
tear apart the veena today, on this day of grief.
From land to land I wander, singing the song of your sorrow
through cities, plains, and forest after forest. Tears fall from both eyes;
hearts of stone weep to hear that tale.
Ten thousand souls blaze up and, joined together, sing one song—
fire gleams in their eyes—the void trembles with a sky-piercing thunderclap!
All gaze on in silence, in fear.
Brother, friend—apart from you I have no one.
You are father, you are mother, you are my all.
For your sorrow I will weep, Mother, for your sorrow I will make others weep.
For you I have kept this life, for you I will lay it down.
All sorrows I will gladly bear,
gazing upon your face.
We have bound a thousand hearts with a single thread,
we have pledged a thousand lives to a single cause—
Bande Mataram.
Let a thousand obstacles come, let doomsday break,
we, a thousand souls, will stand unafraid—
Bande Mataram.
We will not fear the storm and tempest,
ten thousand waves we will bear on our breasts with ease.
If this mortal life must break, let it break,
yet this firm bond will never be torn—
Bande Mataram.
For you, Mother, I have offered this body. For you, Mother, I have offered my life.
For your grief these eyes will rain tears; this veena will sing its song for you.
Though this arm is feeble and weak, it will do your work.
Though this sword is dulled with tarnish, it will destroy your bonds.
Though, O goddess, my blood can gain you nothing,
still, O Mother, I can pour it out to wash away one grain of your stain—
to quench your torment.
Though, Mother, though this veena of mine has little power,
who knows, Mother—one child yet may wake on hearing this veena's strain.
Yet I cannot offer up my life.
Better to die moment by moment, bearing insult at every step.
Neatly woven words, rounds of wailing—yet no one's eyes hold tears.
Carrying and carrying the tray of petitions and pleas, the head bows low.
Begging affection with tears—shame, oh what shame! Dressed as a beggar before the world—
we do not do our own work, and sulk at others instead.
Set down your load of shame yourself; go not to another's door—
to clasp another's feet and beg for honor is the basest of all begging.
Trailing after others crying 'Give, give,' you gain nothing at all—
you want honor, you want life—first give your life away.
Why do you gaze, O Mother, into their faces?
They do not want you, want you not; they do not know their own mother.
They will give you nothing, nothing—they only speak lies in so many guises.
You keep giving, Mother, all that is yours—your golden harvests, the Ganga's waters,
knowledge, faith, so many holy tales.
What will they give you? Nothing, nothing. They will only speak lies from mean souls.
Keep your heart's pain, Mother, in your heart. Hold back the tears within your eyes.
Hide your face, Mother, on your bed of dust—forget your unworthy children.
Gazing at the void, counting the hours, see whether the long night will pass.
What use, Mother, to tell your sorrow to pitiless, senseless stone?
Once, all of you, call out 'Mother'—let it soothe the ears of the world,
let the Himalayan rock weep and melt—lift up your faces today and look.
Stand up now, forgetting self and other; let lightning leap from heart to heart—
raising ten million heads to the morning sky, sing out fearless today.
If two hundred million voices call out 'Mother,' a thrill will run through the endless universe;
if two hundred million children gather round their mother, the ten directions will smile with joy.
That morning a new sun will sow new life;
this is no tale, this is no dream—that day will come, it will come.
When you call your own mother 'Mother,' when you hold your own brother in your heart,
all sin and anguish drift far away on the breeze of holy love.
There the gods' blessing abides—no quarrel remains, no sorrow remains—
insult is ended, the soul awakes, and stainless genius unfolds.
Who comes and goes, again and again, with anguished tears in her eyes?
Who gazes into our faces, full of hope in vain?
She is my mother.
Whose nectar-sweet voice fades away, meeting with neglect?
Whose tongue, alas, would everyone forget?
She is my mother.
Leaving her tender lap but a moment, we can no longer recognize her.
Her own children heap insult on her—
She is my mother.
Who sits sorrowful in the holy hut, setting out the meal?
That loving offering no longer pleases our lips.
She is my mother.
O India, in your court today, hear this poet's song.
To your feet, in fresh joy, we have brought our offering of worship.
We have brought the strength of our bodies, we have brought the devotion of our hearts,
we have brought our faith's resolve, we have brought our lives—
we have brought our finest tribute to give to you.
We have no golden platter; even food is hard to come by.
What we have, we have brought arrayed on a fresh cup of leaves.
No need for pomp today—this is the poor man's worship, a poor man's provision—
we will end our endless poverty by gathering the dust of your feet.
Your grace, rare even to the gods, we will receive in our cup of leaves.
You are no king, O great ascetic—you are the beloved of our souls.
Casting off our beggar's finery, we will wear your mantle.
In poverty lies your treasure; hidden within silence
is your mantra, your word of fire—give us that.
Casting off another's attire, we will wear your mantle.
Give us your mantra of fearlessness, your mantra beyond grief.
Give us the mantra of immortality; give us new life.
The life that dwelt in your hermitage groves, the life that sat on your royal throne—
with that free, radiant, mighty life we will fill our hearts.
Death-crossing, dread-dispelling—give us that mantra of yours.
In the new year we have made a vow: we will take our own land's initiation—
in your ashram, at your feet, O India, we will take our schooling.
Another's ornaments, another's garments—today we will renounce another's food—
if we must be poor we will not be base; we will give up begging from others.
In the new year we have made a vow: we will take our own land's initiation.
If there is no palace, there is still the hut, hallowed by blessing.
If there is no city, there is your forest, wondrous with fruit and flower.
The farther we have moved away from you, the smaller we have seen you.
Seen near today, O king of hearts, you are our friend of old.
O ascetic, your leaf-thatched hut is hallowed by blessing.
Turned strangers to you by another's words, we have given and received shame.
To forget you we turned our faces away and put on another's attire.
Counting nothing, saying nothing, you chant your mantra deep within—
your eternal seat of meditation is our very bone and marrow.
Forgetting you for another's speech, we have given and received shame.
All that shame we will renounce today; we will take your initiation.
Sitting apart at your feet, we will learn your teaching.
Your faith, your work, the deep meaning of your mantra—
we will take them up, forgetting all else, giving up begging from others.
In your glory we will take our pride; we will take your initiation.
O brother, do not fret in vain.
What cannot be will never be, by any means—we will not let it be.
We will not fall sprawling in the dust; the bond will not break—we will not let it go.
We will take on our heads no burden that would bow them down.
Sorrow there is; sorrow must be borne—
however far there is to go, that way must be gone.
Looking upward, oh, take the pain and hold it to your breast—take it, everyone.
He who is the helper of the helpless—your anguish will strike home to him.
Today let everyone come running together, wherever each may be—
now let whoever wishes cut their bonds; we will bind our Mother.
With our lives we will make her our own, binding her with the cord of truth,
binding her in her children's embrace with a hundred thousand coils.
Today rich and poor are all equal. Come, Hindu; come, Muslim—
today let all work lie where it is—come in your hundreds of thousands.
Today throw open everyone's doors; go, forgetting every care—
above every other call, today our Mother calls us.
